summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to handle and lift steel, cylinders, gates and fabrications safely, and to lead others in doing so. You will learn how handling injuries happen, how to assess a task with the TILE headings, how to lift, carry, push and pull safely and teach it, how to plan team lifts, how to choose and use handling aids, how to work out weights and sling loads, how to check lifting gear and rig a load, and how to plan lifts, supervise and report.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). In a fabrication shop almost everything is heavy, long, sharp or awkward: plate, pipe, angle, gas cylinders, gates, frames and boxes of electrodes. Handling them is one of the main causes of injury to welders, and back injuries can end a working life.

At Level 3 you do more than lift safely yourself. You **assess** handling tasks, **choose** aids and methods, **work out** weights and sling loads, **plan and lead** team lifts and lifts with a chain block, **check** lifting gear, **teach and supervise** others, and **report and investigate** when something goes wrong.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and leading hands and supervisors in Jamaican fabrication shops, stores and sites.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Understand the risks and duties
Explain how handling injuries happen, their early signs, and the duties of employers, leaders and workers.
Assess handling tasks
Use the TILE headings (task, individual, load, environment) to find the risks and record the controls.
Lift, carry, push and pull safely
Use and teach a safe technique, and spot and correct poor technique.
Plan team lifts
Decide when a team carry is safe, choose and brief the team, and give the commands.
Choose and use handling aids
Pick the right trolley, truck, clamp, magnet, hoist or forklift for the load, and use it within its rating.
Work out weights and sling loads
Calculate the mass of steel and of the whole load, find the centre of gravity and the load in each sling leg.
Check gear and rig loads
Inspect slings, shackles, hooks and chain blocks before use, take faulty gear out of service, and rig, trial-lift and land a load safely.
Plan, supervise and report
Write a lift plan, give roles, supervise, and report and investigate injuries and near misses.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on duties, risk assessment, handling aids, lifting gear, technique, team lifting, weight calculations, sling angles, rigging, health and injury, reporting, supervision and planning a lift.

A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and quick sums, such as WLL, centre of gravity, spreader beam, tag line, lever hoist, gantry, near miss) and essays on a TILE assessment, the order of controls, teaching a lift, a team carry, choosing aids, checking gear, sling angles, preventing injury, dealing with an injury and site conditions.

**Practical tasks**: a TILE assessment and planned move of mixed steel stock with handling aids, each member leading one item; and a planned lift of a welded frame with a chain block, slings and shackles, with gear checks and a lift record.

blocks.note: Learn the reasons, not only the rules. Many questions ask which method is **safest** or **best** for a given load, place and team, or what a leader should do next.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Handling injuries and who must do what

blocks.p: **Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs)** are injuries and pain in the muscles, tendons, joints, nerves and the back. In fabrication work they affect the lower back most, and also the neck, shoulders, arms, wrists and knees.

The spine is a column of bones (vertebrae) with soft, cushioning **discs** between them. Lifting with a bent back, twisting, or holding a load far from the body puts very large forces on the lower discs. A disc can bulge or burst and press on a nerve, which is a **slipped (herniated) disc**, causing back pain and pain or numbness down the leg.

head: Causes in fabrication work
Early warning signs
rows: Lifting heavy or awkward steel
Stooping, twisting, reaching
Holding loads away from the body
Repeating the same movement for hours (grinding, hammering, carrying)
Cramped positions under a job
Tiredness, heat and rushing
Aches or stiffness that last after work
Pain when bending or getting up
Tingling or numbness in the hands or legs
Weakness or poor grip
Poor sleep because of pain

blocks.note: Injuries often build up over weeks before one lift 'does it'. Report aches early: the cause can then be fixed before it becomes a long-term injury.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: **Avoid** manual handling where it can be avoided: for example have the supplier's crane truck place steel straight onto the racks, or cut and weld parts where they will be used
**Assess** the handling that cannot be avoided: look at the task, the individual, the load and the environment, and write it down
**Reduce** the risk as low as is reasonably possible: handling aids, smaller loads, team lifts, better routes and storage, training
**Review** the controls: check they work and update them when things change

head: Who
Main duties
rows: Employer and the Centre
Avoid hazardous handling where possible; assess what cannot be avoided; provide aids, safe systems, training and supervision; keep lifting equipment examined and maintained
Team leader or supervisor
Plan the work; carry out and share the risk assessments; choose methods; brief and supervise; stop unsafe work; report and investigate
Worker or trainee
Follow the safe system; use the aids and PPE given; not take on loads beyond what is safe; report aches, injuries, near misses and faulty equipment; never interfere with safety equipment

blocks.note: Jamaica's workplace safety laws (such as the factories law and its regulations) and every employer's safety policy place duties on both employers and workers, and inspectors from the Ministry of Labour and Social Security visit workplaces. Your instructor will explain which rules apply to the Centre and to your workplace.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **manual handling risk assessment** looks at four things, remembered as **TILE**. Watch the job being done and talk to the people who do it.

head: Heading
Questions to ask
Example from the shop
rows: **T**ask
How far, how often, how long? Is there stooping, twisting, reaching, holding at arm's length, lifting from the floor or above the shoulders? Are there rest breaks? Is it rushed?
Carrying 6 m pipe 30 m from the yard to the saw, ten times a morning
**I**ndividual
Who does it? Training, experience, health, past injury, pregnancy, size and strength? Does it need unusual strength?
A trainee back at work after a back strain
**L**oad
How heavy (work it out)? Size and shape? Long, wide or thin enough to catch the wind? Stable? Sharp, hot, oily or hard to grip? Where is the heavy end?
A thin 2.4 m sheet that catches the wind; a gate with a heavy hinge side
**E**nvironment
Route, floor, steps, slopes, doors, corners, space to turn, light, heat, rain, wind, other traffic
An oily patch and a step on the way to the bay; the midday sun in an open yard

blocks.p: There is no single safe weight. A common guide (the filter used in many training courses) is about **25 kg** for men and **16 kg** for women, for a load held **close to the body at waist height**. The figure falls sharply when the load is held away from the body, low near the floor, or above the shoulders, and falls further when the person twists or lifts often. Anything over the guide needs a detailed assessment and, usually, an aid.

head: Team size
Common guide for the team's capacity
rows: Two people
About **two-thirds** of what they could each lift alone, added together. Two people who can each manage 20 kg: about 2/3 × 40 = 27 kg
Three people
About **half** of the total. Three people at 20 kg each: about 1/2 × 60 = 30 kg
Four or more
Rarely practical: people cannot all grip well or move together; use an aid

blocks.p: Two people cannot safely lift twice what one can: they seldom share the weight evenly or move exactly together, and one may slip or stop.

head: Condition
Risk
Control
rows: Heat and strong sun
Tiredness, sweat and poor grip; steel left in the sun burns hands
Heavy handling in the cooler morning; water and shaded breaks; shared work; gloves
Rain
Slippery steel, mud and boots; soft ground
Stop heavy handling in heavy rain; wipe loads; boards or gravel on the route
Rough ground and slopes
Trips, loss of balance; trolleys hard to push or run away
A firm, level, cleared route; boards or ramps; wheeled aids only where the ground suits them
Tight space
Twisting and stooping
Clear room to work; set loads down near where they are needed; lifting aids
Poor light
Hidden steps, cables and offcuts
Lighting; work in daylight
Wind
Sheets act like sails and can pull people over
Carry sheets on edge, in pairs, and not in strong wind

ul: Write down each risk, the control chosen, who is responsible, the date and your name.
Share the assessment with the team, and keep a copy where the work is done.
Review it after an injury or near miss, when the task, people or place change, and at set times.

blocks.h: A safe lift from the floor

flow: Think first: check the load's weight, stability, grip, sharp or oily edges; check the route and where it will go; get help or an aid if needed
Stand close to the load, feet apart, one foot slightly forward, for a steady base
Bend the knees and hips; keep the back in its natural curve (do not stoop)
Get a firm grip with the whole hand, wearing gloves if the edges are sharp or rough; keep the heaviest side next to you
Lift smoothly by straightening the legs, head up, without jerking
Keep the load close to your waist as you carry it
Turn by moving your feet, never by twisting the trunk
Put it down by bending the knees; set it down first, then slide it into place

blocks.note: A load held at arm's length is far harder on the back than the same load held close: the strain on the lower back grows with the distance of the load from the body.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Carry close to the body, and never so high or so stacked that you cannot see where you are going: split the load or use a trolley.
Do not carry a load up or down steps or ladders if it can be lifted or passed up another way.
Rest before you are tired, especially in the heat.
**Push** rather than pull where you can: you can use your body weight, keep your back straight and see where you are going.
Keep trolleys and pallet trucks well maintained, with sound wheels and correct tyre pressure.
On a ramp or slope, keep yourself on the **uphill** side of the load, so it cannot run over you: going down, the hand truck goes in front of you and you hold it back; going up, you are above it.
Never let a loaded trolley run on its own.
Store the heaviest items at about **waist height**, lighter items higher or lower.
Keep long bar and pipe on racks at waist height, not on the floor.
Set jobs on stands or trestles at a good working height, so welders do not stoop for hours.
Use a step platform, never a box or a chair, to reach high shelves, and do not lift heavy items above the shoulders.

flow: Explain why each step matters
Show the lift yourself, step by step
Let the trainee try while you watch
Correct faults at once, calmly, and let them try again
Check again later on real jobs, without warning
Record the training and the checks

blocks.p: If you see someone lifting badly, for example with a bent back and straight legs, stop them before they lift, show them the right way and watch them do it. Shouting across the shop or writing them up without a word teaches nothing.

blocks.note: Back-support belts are **not** a control: there is no good evidence that they prevent injury, and they can make people feel they can lift more. They never replace aids, safe technique and limits.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Team lifting and long or awkward loads

blocks.p: First work out the weight, and ask whether an aid would be better: a trolley, bar dollies, a gantry or a forklift. Choose a team carry only for a load that the team guide allows and that cannot sensibly go on an aid.

blocks.h: Planning and leading a team carry

flow: Work out the weight and check it is within the team's capacity
Choose enough people of similar height and build, all trained, wearing gloves and safety boots
Walk the route first: clear it, and check doors, corners, steps, slopes and where the load will be set down
Brief the team: who holds where, the route, and the commands, such as 'Ready, lift', 'Walk', 'Stop', 'Lower'
One person (the leader) gives every command
Lift together on the command, keep the load level, walk in step, and stop at corners to plan the turn
Lower together on the command, onto packing if fingers could be trapped
Afterwards, talk about what went well and what to change

head: Load
Method
rows: 6 m lengths of pipe or section
Bar dollies, a long trolley or a pipe rack on wheels. For a team carry, people on the same shoulder or the same side, the leader at the front calling the moves; watch the ends at corners and doorways
Thin sheets (for example 2.4 × 1.2 m)
Sheet clamps or a sheet trolley. By hand: two people, cut-resistant gloves, the sheet carried on edge, never flat overhead or dragged; not in strong wind
Bundles of short bar
Kept bundled and moved on a trolley or pallet; not carried loose
Finished gates and frames
A gantry or forklift for loading; a planned team carry with a leader only for lighter gates; packing at the truck bed
Gas cylinders
A cylinder trolley, upright and chained; never rolled flat or carried by the valve

blocks.note: Hot steel looks like cold steel. Before handling anything that has been welded, cut, or lying in the sun, check it, and wear gloves.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Aid
Good for
Watch out
rows: Flat trolley, pallet truck
Boxes, pallets and bundles over smooth, level floors
Small wheels sink in gravel and soft ground; rated load; push, do not pull
Bar dollies, long trolleys
Long bar and pipe
Load secured so it cannot roll off
Two-wheel hand truck
Boxes and drums
Keep uphill of it on slopes; strap the load
Cylinder trolley
Gas cylinders
Upright and chained
Plate clamp
Lifting **one** plate at a time from a hook
Never two plates at once: the lower plate is not gripped and can slide out; the clamp must suit the plate thickness and the lift (vertical or horizontal)
Lifting magnet
Quick lifting of clean, flat plate
Rated for a stated thickness and condition: thin, curved, painted, rusty or rough plate grips less; never over people
Rollers, crowbars and jacks
Moving heavy machine bases short distances; levering an edge up so packing can go under
Hands and feet clear of rollers; steer with a bar; block the load as it is raised
Chain block
Lifting and lowering loads on a gantry or beam
Rated (SWL or WLL) for the load; brake works; check before use
Lever hoist (come-along)
Pulling or lifting along a chain at any angle, for example aligning a base
Rated load; never extend the lever with a pipe
Gantry or A-frame
A beam on legs or wheels from which a chain block hangs
Rated for the load plus the block and slings; level, firm ground
Spreader (lifting) beam
Keeps sling legs upright and spreads the lifting points on long loads
Its own rating; counts in the total load
Forklift
Pallets and heavy bundles
**Only a trained, authorised driver**; nobody rides on the forks; loads carried low

ul: Match the aid to the load (weight, shape, length), the distance, the floor and the space.
Check the aid's rating is more than the load, including pallets, slings and the block.
Make sure the people using it are trained and the aid has been inspected.
Example: a 400 kg welded frame onto stands in the workshop needs a rated chain block on a gantry with rated slings, not six trainees or a car jack.

blocks.p: A chain block trades distance for force: you pull a lot of hand chain to raise the load a little. If a block raises its load 30 mm for every metre of hand chain pulled, raising the load 1 m needs 1 000 ÷ 30 = about 33 m of hand chain. Plan the time, and never try to speed it up by pulling the load chain.

sections.title: Weights, centre of gravity and sling loads

ul: **Plate:** length (m) × width (m) × thickness (m) × 7 850 kg/m³. A plate 2.4 m × 1.2 m × 6 mm: 2.4 × 1.2 × 0.006 × 7 850 = about 136 kg.
**Sections:** length × mass per metre from the steel tables. A 6 m length of angle at 3.8 kg/m: 6 × 3.8 = 22.8 kg.
**A fabrication:** list every piece from the drawing, find each mass, add them, and add a little for welds and fittings.
**Total load on the hook:** the load + the pallet or packing + the slings, shackles and any spreader beam. Five bars at 30 kg on a 15 kg pallet with 5 kg of slings: 150 + 15 + 5 = 170 kg.

blocks.p: The **centre of gravity (CG)** is the point through which the whole weight of a load seems to act. For a plain bar or plate it is in the middle; for a frame with a heavy end (a motor mount, a hinge side) it is nearer the heavy end. Hang the hook **directly above the CG**; otherwise the load tilts or swings as it leaves the ground. If it tilts, lower it, move the hook or adjust the slings, and try again.

blocks.h: The load in each sling leg

blocks.p: When two sling legs hang straight down, each carries half the load. When the legs spread out, each leg pulls partly sideways as well as up. Only the upward part holds the load, so the pull in each leg must grow.
**Load in each leg = (load ÷ 2) ÷ cos (half the angle between the legs)**

head: Angle between the legs
Load in each leg
For a 1 000 kg load
rows: 0° (legs vertical)
0.5 × load
500 kg
0.58 × load
580 kg
0.71 × load
710 kg
1.0 × load
1 000 kg in **each** leg

blocks.note: Most multi-leg slings are rated for angles up to 90° between the legs. Never rig wider than the tag allows: use longer legs or a **spreader beam** to keep the angle small.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The way a sling is used changes what it can carry. A **choke hitch** (the sling wrapped round the load and through its own eye) usually reduces the working load limit to about 80% of a straight lift; a **basket** with vertical legs can carry about twice. Use the factors on the sling's tag or the maker's chart.

flow: Work out the total weight of the load
Find the CG and choose the lifting points
Measure the distance between lifting points and decide the leg length, so the angle is within the rating
Choose slings and shackles whose rating, at that angle and hitch, is more than the load
Check edges that need protection

ul: Every item of lifting gear is marked with an identity number and its **safe working load (SWL)** or **working load limit (WLL)**: the most it may lift in normal use.

Gear is given a **thorough examination** by a competent person at set intervals (often every 6 months for slings and accessories and every 12 months for hoists, or as the law and the Centre's rules say), and the date is recorded on a tag or register.
The **user** checks every item by eye **before each use**.

head: Item
Reject it if you find
rows: Chain sling
Stretched, bent, twisted, nicked, gouged or worn links; damaged hooks or master link; no tag
Wire rope sling
Broken wires, kinks, crushing, birdcaging (strands opened out), heavy rust, damaged eyes or ferrules
Webbing or round sling
Cuts, tears, burns, chemical damage, worn stitching, a missing or unreadable label
Shackle
Bent or worn body; the wrong pin, or a bolt in place of the pin; a pin that will not screw fully home
Hook
Opened out (throat stretched), twisted, cracked; safety latch missing or not closing
Chain block
Brake slipping, damaged chain or hooks, jammed or rough operation, no tag or out of date

blocks.note: Faulty, untagged or out-of-date gear is taken out of use **at once**, tagged DO NOT USE, kept apart and reported. Never tie a knot in a sling, tape over damage, or write a new rating on it. A competent person decides whether it is repaired or destroyed, and the register is updated.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Screw shackle pins **fully home**, and use the correct pin for the shackle.
Make sure hook latches close, so the sling cannot slip off.
Fit packing or edge guards where a sling passes over a sharp edge.
Hang the hook directly above the CG.
Fit a **tag line** to a long or swinging load, so a person can steady it from a safe distance. Hold it; never wrap it round the hand or tie it to yourself.

flow: Set up an exclusion zone with barriers; nobody stands or walks under the load
Brief the team on the plan, the roles and the signals
Trial lift: raise the load just a few centimetres and hold it; check the balance, the slings and the brake
If it tilts or anything slips, lower it and correct it
Raise and move the load smoothly, with the tag line holder steadying it
Lower onto stands or packing, keeping hands and feet out of the gap between the load and the stands
Let the slings go slack before removing them
Store the gear clean and dry; report any damage

ul: **One named person** gives signals to the operator, using agreed signals or words, so the operator never gets two instructions at once.
**Anyone** who sees danger may give the **stop** signal, and it is obeyed at once.
A load is **never left hanging** unattended, not even for a short break: lower it and set it down first.

blocks.p: Before any lift with a chain block or other lifting equipment, or any heavy move (for example a 300 kg fabrication out to a truck), the team leader prepares a simple **lift plan**:

ul: The load and its weight, with the working; the CG
The equipment: gantry, chain block, slings, shackles, spreader, with their ratings and the sling angle
The route, the landing place and the exclusion zone
The roles: lift leader (gives signals), operator, rigger, tag-line holder, area guard and recorder
The signals and the stop rule
What happens if something goes wrong
Watch handling across the shop, not only planned lifts.
Correct poor technique at once by showing the right way.
Rotate heavy and repetitive tasks, plan breaks and water in the heat, and keep aids available and in good order.
Encourage people to report aches early, and act on them.

flow: Stop the work and make the area safe

See to the injured person: call the first aider; do not move them if they cannot move themselves; get medical help (in Jamaica, dial 110 for an ambulance) if the pain is severe or there is numbness, tingling or weakness
If they can walk, they rest and are sent to a doctor or clinic for a check
Write the accident report the same day: name, date, time, place, what they were doing, what happened, the injury, the first aid given, witnesses
Investigate why it happened: the load, the method, the people, the aids available, the route, the training, the plan
Decide actions to stop it happening again, update the risk assessment, brief the team, and follow up

blocks.p: A **near miss** is an event that could have caused an injury or damage but did not, for example a chain block that slips and lets a load drop 100 mm. Treat it seriously: stop using the equipment, tag it out, report it and find the cause. Near misses are free warnings.

Ask 'why?' until you reach something the organisation can change. 'He did not bend his knees' is rarely the whole story: why was the load lifted by hand at all? Was the aid available? Was the job planned? Was there time pressure? The best actions change the system (planned methods, aids booked, better storage), not just the person.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what MSDs and a slipped disc are, and name their causes and early signs.
I can explain the order avoid, assess, reduce, review, with workshop examples.
I can state the duties of employers, leaders and workers.
I can carry out and record a TILE risk assessment.
I can explain the guide weights and the team guides of two-thirds and one-half.
I can control the risks of heat, rain, rough ground, slopes, tight space, poor light and wind.
I can lift, carry, push and pull safely, including on ramps.
I can teach a safe lift and check that it has been learned.
I can plan and lead a team carry of a long or awkward load.
I can choose the right handling aid for plate, bar, pipe, cylinders, pallets and frames.
I can work out the weight of plate, sections and a whole load on the hook.
I can find the centre of gravity and work out the load in each sling leg.
I can choose a sling for the angle and hitch.
I can inspect slings, shackles, hooks and chain blocks, and deal with faulty gear.
I can rig a load, carry out a trial lift, use a tag line and land a load safely.
I can give and follow lifting signals.
I can write a lift plan with roles.
I can deal with an injury, report it, find the real cause and act on it.

terms: Bar dollies
Small wheeled supports for moving long bar and pipe
Centre of gravity (CG)
The point through which a load's whole weight seems to act
Chain block
A hand-operated hoist that lifts a load on a chain
Choke hitch
A sling wrapped round a load and through its own eye; it lowers the sling's capacity
Crowbar
A long steel bar for levering up the edge of a heavy load
Exclusion zone
The barriered area round a lift that nobody may enter
Gantry
A frame with a beam across the top from which a chain block hangs
Lever hoist
A hand-lever tool that pulls or lifts along a chain at any angle
Lift plan
The written plan for a lift: load, gear, angle, route, zone and roles
MSD
Musculoskeletal disorder: pain or injury in muscles, joints, nerves or the back
Near miss
An event that could have caused injury or damage but did not
Plate clamp
A clamp that grips a single plate for lifting
Shackle
A U-shaped connector closed by a screw pin
Slipped disc
A spinal disc that bulges out and presses on a nerve
Spreader beam
A beam that keeps sling legs upright and spreads the lifting points
SWL / WLL
Safe working load / working load limit: the most a piece of gear may lift in normal use
Tag line
A rope on a load so a person can steady it from a safe distance
Thorough examination
A periodic, recorded inspection of lifting gear by a competent person
TILE
Task, Individual, Load, Environment: the headings of a handling risk assessment
Trial lift
Raising a load a few centimetres to check balance, slings and brake

c1.title: Unloading a mixed delivery at a training centre in Stony Hill
c1.text: A truck arrives at a training centre in Stony Hill, St Andrew, with steel for the Level 3 group: 6 m lengths of 100 mm hollow tube weighing about 9.5 kg per metre, 1220 × 2440 mm sheets of 1.5 mm plate, bundles of short flat bar, and a 480 kg pallet of electrode boxes. The truck must park on gravel 25 m from the store, which has a smooth concrete floor. The centre has a pallet truck and a forklift with two trained, authorised drivers. Kemoy, the student team leader, plans the move with three classmates who can each manage about 25 kg alone. One of them, Tanya, strained her back last month.

c2.title: Lifting a pump base frame near Grange Hill
c2.text: At a waterworks workshop near Grange Hill, Westmoreland, Nordia's team must lift a welded pump base frame of about 600 kg onto stands with a chain block on a gantry rated at 1 000 kg. They will use a two-leg chain sling with the legs at 60° to each other, and a tag line. The lift plan names Nordia as lift leader and Junior as chain block operator. Half-way through the job, with the frame hanging 300 mm above the floor, the team is called to lunch.

c3.title: A strained back at a gate shop in Lionel Town
c3.text: At a gate shop in Lionel Town, Clarendon, Ricardo strains his back while he and one other welder lift a 90 kg gate onto a truck. The shop has a gantry with a chain block, but it was being used on another job, so they 'just lifted it'. Ricardo is in severe pain and cannot stand up straight. Afterwards, two other welders say their backs have ached for weeks from carrying gates.

c4.title: Racks and trolleys in a steel store in Duncans
c4.text: Nicola is reorganising the steel store at a fabrication shop in Duncans, Trelawny. Heavy boxes of bolts and electrodes are kept on the top shelf, about 1.9 m high, and light boxes of gloves at waist height. Every delivery of steel is carried in by hand from the road. A ramp leads down from the store to the workshop, and the team takes boxes down it on a two-wheel hand truck.

c5.title: Training a new trainee in Linstead
c5.text: At a fabrication shop in Linstead, St Catherine, Andre has been asked to train Shamar, a new trainee, in manual handling. Shamar has bought a back-support belt and says he will not need the trolleys if he wears it. In his first week, Andre sees him carrying two boxes of parts stacked so high that he cannot see over them.

questions.q: About how much does one sheet of the 1.5 mm plate weigh?
o: About 4.5 kg
About 35 kg
About 23 kg
About 70 kg
questions.why: 1.22 × 2.44 × 0.0015 × 7 850 = about 35 kg. That is over the guide for one person carrying an awkward sheet, so it needs two people or a sheet trolley. 23 kg and 70 kg are the masses of 1 mm and 3 mm sheets.

questions.q: Using the common guide that three people can handle about half of their combined capacity, can three classmates carry one length of the tube?
o: Yes: three people can manage 75 kg between them
Yes: the tube is long, so each end is quite light
No: three people should never carry tube together
No: the guide gives about 37 kg, so use an aid
questions.why: One length weighs about 6 × 9.5 = 57 kg. Three people rarely share a load evenly or move exactly together, so the guide allows about half of 3 × 25 = 75 kg, which is about 37 kg. Bar dollies or a long trolley are needed.

questions.q: What is the best way to get the 480 kg pallet into the store?
o: A trained forklift driver moves it
Pull it across the gravel on the pallet truck
Unpack it and carry the boxes in one by one
Slide it off the tailgate and roll it on bars
questions.why: Pallet trucks have small wheels that sink and stick in gravel, and carrying the boxes means dozens of lifts in the heat. A trained, authorised forklift driver can take the whole pallet across the gravel; the pallet truck can then move it on the concrete.

questions.q: Under which TILE heading should Kemoy record Tanya's back strain last month?
o: Task
Load
Individual
Environment
questions.why: Health, past injury, training and strength belong under Individual. Kemoy should give Tanya work that suits her and get advice before she does heavy handling.

questions.q: About what load is in each leg of the sling?
o: About 300 kg
About 600 kg
About 350 kg
About 175 kg
questions.why: With the legs vertical each would carry 300 kg. At 60° between the legs, each leg also pulls sideways, so each carries 300 ÷ cos 30° = 300 ÷ 0.866 = about 346 kg. The sling must be rated for that at this angle.

questions.q: Who should give signals to Junior during the lift?
o: Nordia only; anyone may call stop
Whoever is standing nearest to the frame
Each person, for their own side of the frame
Nobody: Junior decides for himself as he goes
questions.why: Signals come from one named person, so the operator never gets two different instructions at once. Stop is the exception: anyone who sees danger may give it, and it is obeyed at once.

questions.q: How should the tag line be used?
o: Wrapped round the hand, so the grip cannot slip off
Tied to the gantry leg so the frame cannot swing
Pulled hard to bring one side of the frame level
Held at a distance, never wrapped round the hand
questions.why: A tag line lets a person steady or turn the load from outside its reach. Wrapped round the hand, a swinging or dropping load can drag the person in. A load that hangs crooked is lowered and re-rigged, not pulled level.

questions.q: What should happen to the frame when the team is called to lunch?
o: Leave it hanging with the chain block's brake on
Lower it onto stands or packing first
Leave it hanging with barrier tape round it
Raise it higher so nobody can walk into it
questions.why: A suspended load must never be left unattended: a brake can slip, and someone may walk under it. It is lowered and set down safely before anyone leaves.

questions.q: What should the team leader do first?
o: Make it safe; get first aid and medical help
Write the accident report while it is fresh
Find out who decided to lift the gate by hand
Help Ricardo stand up and walk it off
questions.why: The injured person comes first. With severe pain he should not be moved or made to walk; the first aider is called and medical help sought. The report and the investigation follow the same day.

questions.q: Which finding gets nearest to the real cause of the injury?
o: Ricardo did not bend his knees enough on the lift
The gate was heavier than Ricardo had expected
Loading had no planned method or booked aid
The truck was parked too far from the shop door
questions.why: The lift happened because loading gates depended on whoever was free, and the gantry was not planned in. Blaming technique misses the system fault; the fix is a planned loading method with the aid booked, or a second aid.

questions.q: What do the other welders' aching backs tell the team leader?
o: Aching backs are normal for welders and need no action
The way gates are handled is hurting several people
Those two welders should be given light work for good
They should all start wearing back-support belts
questions.why: Lasting aches are early signs of musculoskeletal injury. When several people report them, the task itself needs reassessing and changing, and the welders should be encouraged to see a doctor.

questions.q: Which change to the shelving does most to cut the handling risk?
o: A step-stool by the top shelf for the heavy boxes
A sign on the shelf giving each box's weight
A non-slip mat on the floor below the top shelf
Heavy boxes at waist height, light ones up high
questions.why: Lifting heavy loads above shoulder height puts great strain on the back and shoulders, and a dropped box can injure. Storing the heaviest items at about waist height removes that strain at its source.

questions.q: How should a loaded hand truck be taken down the ramp to the workshop?
o: With the worker downhill, walking backwards
Let it roll down on its own and catch it
As fast as possible so it does not tip over
Worker uphill, holding the load back
questions.why: Keep yourself on the uphill side, so that if the load runs away it does not run over you: going down, the truck goes in front and you hold it back. Never let a loaded truck run on its own.

questions.q: Which change would avoid most of the hand carrying of steel deliveries?
o: Have the team carry the steel in faster, in pairs
Suppliers crane bundles straight onto racks
Give everyone back belts for delivery days
Move deliveries to the cooler early morning
questions.why: Avoiding the handling comes first in the order of control. A supplier's crane truck placing bundles directly onto racks by the door takes away most of the lifting; carrying faster or wearing belts does not.

questions.q: How should Andre respond to the back-support belt?
o: Let him wear it in place of using the trolleys
Ban the belt and say nothing more about it
Explain belts do not replace safe methods
Order belts for every worker in the shop
questions.why: There is no good evidence that back belts prevent injury, and they can make people feel they can lift more. Andre should explain why the trolleys, the safe method and the limits still apply.

questions.q: What should Shamar do instead of carrying the stacked boxes?
o: Split the load or use a trolley, to see ahead
Carry both, since two boxes save a second trip
Carry them on one shoulder instead
Hold them out at arm's length to see past
questions.why: A load he cannot see over hides steps, cables and people, and a stack is unstable. Splitting the load or using a trolley keeps the route in view; holding loads at arm's length adds strain to the back.

questions.q: How should Andre check that Shamar has really learned to handle loads safely?
o: Have him sign a form saying he understood
Watch him on real jobs over the coming weeks
Give him a written test on the TILE headings
Ask the other trainees if he lifts properly
questions.why: Training works only if it changes what people do. Andre watches Shamar handling real loads, corrects faults at once, and records the training and the checks.

questions.q: A heavy machine base is being moved on steel rollers. Which rule matters most?
o: Keep hands and feet clear of the rollers; steer with a bar
Push from the front of the load so you can see the rollers
Use as few rollers as possible so the base stays level
Place the rollers by hand while the base is still moving
questions.why: Rollers can crush fingers and feet as the load moves onto them. Steer and lever with a bar, place rollers only when the load is stopped and blocked, and never stand in front of a moving load.

questions.q: A chain sling's tag shows its last thorough examination was 14 months ago. The Centre's rule is every 6 months. What should be done?
o: Use it, as long as it looks sound by eye
Use it only for loads under half its rating
Take it out of use until examined
Write today's date on the tag and use it
questions.why: Gear that is out of date for its thorough examination may not be used, however it looks. It is tagged out and kept apart until a competent person has examined it and the record is updated.

questions.q: A webbing sling is marked with a working load limit of 2 000 kg for a straight lift. It is to be used in a choke hitch. About what is its limit now?
o: About 2 000 kg
About 4 000 kg
About 1 000 kg
About 1 600 kg
questions.why: A choke hitch bends and pinches the sling, so its working load limit is usually reduced to about 80%: 2 000 × 0.8 = 1 600 kg. Use the factors on the sling's tag or the maker's chart.
